title: Butter Chicken Is the New Orange Chicken: Why 2026 Is Indian Cuisine's Breakout Year in America
excerpt: From Keralan curries on fast-casual menus to NEXTY Award-winning naan brands, Indian food is finally crossing the mainstream threshold that Chinese and Mexican cuisines crossed decades ago.
body:
For years, the question hovered over the American restaurant industry like the aroma of a perfectly tempered tadka: when will Indian food finally go mainstream? In 2026, the answer appears to be now.

## Fast-Casual Leads the Charge

The clearest signal comes from the fast-casual segment, where Indian-focused chains are expanding at a pace that would have seemed unthinkable five years ago. Curry Up Now, Tarka Indian Kitchen, and The Kati Roll Company are opening new locations with customizable curries, naan wraps, and kati rolls designed for the grab-and-go American palate. The model is familiar — it's the Chipotle playbook applied to Indian food — but the execution finally matches the ambition.

Restaurant Business Online identified Indian cuisine as one of the defining menu trends of 2026, with industry forecasters pointing specifically to Keralan cuisine as a rising star. The prediction builds on years of incremental progress: turmeric lattes becoming coffee-shop staples, naan appearing on pizza-chain menus, and chai moving from exotic curiosity to basic beverage.

But this year feels different. The movement has graduated from individual ingredients crossing over to entire flavour systems being embraced.

## Beyond the Curry House

The shift isn't just about more Indian restaurants — it's about what kind. A new generation of Indian-American operators is deliberately breaking the mould of the traditional curry house. Concepts like Badmaash in Los Angeles offer Punjabi-spiced steak frites and lamb burgers. Indienne in Chicago presents Indian flavours through a fine-dining French lens. These restaurants aren't asking Americans to try Indian food; they're integrating Indian flavours into formats Americans already love.

Non-Indian chains are following suit. P.F. Chang's has branched beyond Chinese to test Indian-inspired dishes. University dining halls are adding Indian-spiced roast turkey and panang curry to their rotations. When institutional food service — historically the last place to take culinary risks — starts serving biryani, the mainstream moment has arrived.

## The Grocery Aisle Confirms the Trend

The packaged-food world is moving in parallel. Truly Indian, a brand under ADF Foods, was named a 2026 NEXTY Awards finalist in two categories for its Tikka Masala Naan and Crispy Chili Mango Chutney. The NEXTY Awards, presented at Natural Products Expo, are a bellwether for what's about to hit mainstream grocery shelves. Truly Indian's vegan, non-GMO, halal-certified frozen naan — produced daily at scale and available nationwide — represents exactly the kind of accessible entry point that turns curious shoppers into regular buyers.

Indian grocery chains themselves are scaling rapidly, with Patel Brothers and competitors opening massive big-box stores designed to attract customers beyond the South Asian community. ShopRite locations in New Jersey now stock freshly prepared dal makhani and vegetable biryani alongside rotisserie chicken.

## The Diaspora Factor

For the 5.5 million Indian Americans watching this unfold, the mainstream moment is bittersweet. There's pride in seeing the cuisine validated, paired with the familiar anxiety of watching beloved foods simplified or misrepresented. Will butter chicken become the next orange chicken — ubiquitous but unrecognizable to anyone who's had the real thing?

The difference, perhaps, is that this wave is being led largely by Indian Americans themselves. Unlike previous crossover moments driven by non-Indian chefs "discovering" Indian spices, 2026's expansion is powered by diaspora entrepreneurs, chefs, and food brands who understand the cuisine from the inside. Maneet Chauhan, the Indian-American chef who won seasons 2 and 5 of Food Network's Tournament of Champions, has been vocal about the need for more Indian representation in competitive cooking — and her Nashville-style hot chicken pakodas demonstrate exactly how Indian flavours can meet American comfort food without losing their soul.

## What's Next

The question is no longer whether Indian food will go mainstream in America — it's what mainstream will look like. Gen Z and millennial preference data shows steady year-over-year growth in demand for Indian fare at restaurants. Fast-casual concepts are proving the unit economics work. And the grocery infrastructure — from big-box Indian supermarkets to Indian-branded products on Walmart shelves — is finally in place.

For NRIs who spent decades explaining what paneer is at office potlucks, the moment carries a quiet satisfaction. The rest of America is catching up to what the diaspora always knew: this is one of the world's great cuisines, and it was only a matter of time.
